On the other hand, with the passage of time, ecological succession may have modified an intervening strip of habitat leaving miles of hostile habitat over which the isolate cannot or is not likely to travel. The same isolation may occur only during the reproductive phase of the annual cycle, but this is sufficient to maintain populations that are taxonomically distinct.
Either as a result of subsequent constraints on the population over long periods of time or merely as a feature of its identity as a new subspecies, the population is frequently compressed into very restricted range by the time it is recognized by taxonomists. Many species and subspecies never have been widespread in distribution. Their restriction to a narrow range leaves them particularly vulnerable to an environmental disaster that may deplete or extirpate the population.
Eighty percent of the species and subspecies included in the 1973\nedition of the U.S. "Red Book" can be considered geographic isolates

(Appendix F). Their habitats are generally atypical of the biomes in which
they are located. Most are located in southern, southwestern and western

States (Appendix G). A single environmental threat, man-madeor natural,
may lead to extinction of the entire species or subspecies. At any rate,
a threat to any part of that population may be sufficient to consider endanger-\ned what is otherwise a healthy population.
One factor that is frequently responsible for isolation of a population is maintenance of a suitable quality of habitat for animals which require an aquatic or moist environment. More than three-quarters of the species and subspecies that are geographically isolated are dependent upon an aquatic environment during all or part of their annual cycle. In many cases the habitat is a small spring or pool or moist area surrounded by miles of completely adverse environment over which migration is impossible for the animal endemic to the site.
